title: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia
backgroundAndFacts:
Thomas Crowther and other petitioners are transgender women who sought to participate in women's collegiate athletics at institutions within the University System of Georgia, including Georgia Tech. They allege that the Board of Regents and the Georgia Tech Athletic Association maintained policies that excluded them from women's sports based on their transgender status, and that such exclusion constitutes sex discrimination prohibited by Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, a federal law that bans sex discrimination in educational programs receiving federal financial assistance.

The petitioners filed suit in federal court, arguing that discriminating against a person because they are transgender is necessarily a form of sex discrimination, relying in part on the Supreme Court's 2020 decision in Bostock v. Clayton County, which held that employment discrimination against transgender individuals violates Title VII's prohibition on sex discrimination. The U.S. District Court ruled against the petitioners, and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that athletic participation policies excluding transgender women from women's sports do not violate Title IX because such policies are based on physiological distinctions rather than pure sex discrimination.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case after the Solicitor General filed a brief expressing the views of the United States, which supported the respondents' position. The case has attracted significant attention from educators, civil rights advocates, women's sports organizations, states, and businesses, resulting in numerous amicus briefs on both sides of the dispute.
legalQuestion: Whether Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits colleges and universities that receive federal funding from excluding transgender women and girls from women's athletic teams and programs.
significance:
This case will resolve a major national controversy over the scope of Title IX's sex discrimination protections as applied to transgender athletes in educational settings. A ruling for the petitioners could require federally funded schools and colleges to allow transgender women to compete on women's athletic teams nationwide, fundamentally reshaping athletic participation policies. A ruling for the respondents could affirm that schools may maintain women's sports rosters based on biological sex without violating federal anti-discrimination law.

The decision will also clarify how the Supreme Court's landmark 2020 Bostock ruling—which extended Title VII employment protections to transgender employees—applies in the educational and athletics context under Title IX. Because virtually every college and K-12 school in the country receives some federal funding and is subject to Title IX, the ruling will have sweeping practical consequences for student athletes, educational institutions, and state legislatures that have passed laws restricting transgender participation in sports.

parties.coreArgument: Excluding transgender women from women's athletic programs is sex discrimination that violates Title IX, because after Bostock v. Clayton County it is settled that discrimination against transgender individuals is inherently based on sex. Policies that bar transgender women from women's sports treat them worse than other women solely because of their sex assigned at birth, which is precisely the kind of discrimination Title IX was enacted to prevent.
supportingPoints: Bostock established that discrimination against transgender people is a form of sex discrimination, and the same logic applies to Title IX, which uses parallel language to Title VII.
Exclusion from women's athletic programs denies transgender women equal educational opportunities and causes concrete harm to their ability to participate fully in school life.

Schools cannot justify transgender exclusion policies by invoking generalized concerns about competitive fairness, especially when individual circumstances vary widely and blanket bans are not narrowly tailored.
Title IX's implementing regulations and decades of enforcement history support reading the statute to protect transgender students from categorical exclusion based on their gender identity.

parties.party: Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, et al.
parties.coreArgument: Title IX permits educational institutions to maintain sex-separated athletic programs based on biological sex in order to provide equal competitive opportunities for women, and excluding transgender women from those programs does not constitute unlawful sex discrimination. Bostock's statutory interpretation in the employment context does not extend to Title IX athletics, where Congress expressly authorized sex-separated teams to remedy historic disparities in women's sports.
supportingPoints: Title IX explicitly allows schools to operate separate athletic teams for males and females, and policies based on biological sex serve the statute's core purpose of ensuring fair competition for women.
Bostock was a narrow statutory interpretation of Title VII in the employment context and does not control the distinct text, structure, and purpose of Title IX in the competitive sports setting.
Allowing transgender women who went through male puberty to compete in women's sports undermines the very competitive equity that Title IX was designed to protect for biological women.

Congress, not the courts, is the appropriate body to update Title IX if it is to be applied to transgender athletes, and numerous states have exercised their own legislative authority to address this issue.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Petitioners argue this decision—holding that Title VII's ban on sex discrimination covers discrimination against transgender employees—compels the same conclusion under Title IX's similar anti-discrimination language.
Relevant to the scope of Title IX's coverage of federally funded educational programs and the breadth of the statute's reach within institutional activities.

citedPrecedents.caseName: North Haven Board of Education v. Bell
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Establishes the Court's foundational approach to interpreting Title IX broadly to cover discrimination based on sex across federally funded educational activities.

Petitioners cite it for the principle that government-sponsored sex-based exclusions must be justified by an exceedingly persuasive justification, relevant to whether blanket bans on transgender athletes can withstand constitutional and statutory scrutiny.
Supports the argument that discrimination based on sex stereotyping and gender nonconformity is a form of illegal sex discrimination, bolstering transgender plaintiffs' claims under Title IX.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Relevant to the degree of deference, if any, courts owe to agency interpretations of Title IX regarding transgender inclusion in athletic programs, though the Court's recent Loper Bright decision has curtailed such deference.
